title: MB9-21926
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I allow this appeal, and I send this matter back to the RPD to be redetermined.

XXXX XXXX is a 46-year-old citizen of Algeria. For 16 years until 2015, he was a XXXX XXXX there. He alleged that he feared persecution by two terrorists and an organised crime group he had investigated, as well as by the government because he organised a demonstration by XXXX XXXX against corruption and their work conditions.

The RPD held that Mr. XXXX was excluded from being a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection because it found there were serious reasons for considering that as a XXXX XXXX he had committed a crime against humanity. The representative of the Minister, who had intervened in the RPD proceedings on that issue, had submitted at the end of the RPD hearing that the evidence did not justify such a finding.1 I agree with the Minister.

Because of its exclusion finding, the RPD did not examine evidence regarding, nor did it decide, whether Mr. XXXX had a well-founded fear of persecution, i.e., it made no inclusion finding. Exclusion - article 1F(a)
In summary, the RPD findings on exclusion were:

The documentary evidence filed by the Minister shows that the Algerian state used violence to maintain power and to control and repress demonstrations during the time Mr. XXXX was a XXXX XXXX. It also established that the security forces used torture in that period, including on detainees arrested at demonstrations where Mr. XXXX was on duty.

Mr. XXXX made a significant personal and knowing contribution to the criminal purpose of the Algerian security forces, particularly during the giant June 2001 demonstrations in Algiers. His XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was assigned to crowd control at those events and to disperse the demonstrators. The security forces killed tens of participants, hundreds were injured, police tortured detainees and several disappeared.

In addition, while in the Judicial Police division from 2007 to 2015, Mr. XXXX was empowered to XXXX XXXX, and he initiated or carried out at least twenty. As torture is carried out in most Algerian police stations, Mr. XXXX would have been aware that this could happen to those he arrested.
The RPD also noted that Mr. XXXX testimony on these matters was often vague and confused. Appellant's position
Counsel submits that:

The exclusion finding centred on Mr. XXXX presence at the 2001 Kabylie demonstrations as a XXXX XXXX. Having only joined the force two years earlier, his contention that he was a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX at this point in his career is reasonable.

In the documents provided by the Minister, there is no evidence that XXXX XXXX in Mr. XXXX XXXX participated in crimes against humanity. What is more, the documents indicate that during the 2001 demonstrations, crimes against humanity were perpetrated by the gendarmes, a separate body operating under the authority of the Ministry of National Defense. There is an important distinction between the civil police and the gendarmes that appears to have been overlooked or misunderstood by the RPD.

There is no evidence that crimes against humanity were systematically committed by low-ranking civil police of officers under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior. In addition, Mr. XXXX mere presence at the demonstrations as a XXXX XXXX engaged in crowd control is not enough to establish personal and knowing participation in crimes against humanity.

Despite the confusion during testimony regarding his authority to make XXXX, it was clearly established that Mr. XXXX only gained the power to make XXXX in 2007 after his transfer to the XXXX XXXX XXXX. ANALYSIS Knowledge of and connection to state crimes related to the June 2001 demonstrations - RPD overall correct about the former but incorrect about the latter

Mr. XXXX testified that, having been in his XXXX XXXX up till June 2001, he had had no access to media and had no idea at that time of the reason for the demonstrations. He said he learned only years later that they stemmed from oppression and the cost of living. Because he was a trainee, he also hadn't known at the time, he said, that a young man had been killed earlier that year by the police or gendarmerie.2

He also said he had not seen demonstrators at the June 2001 event having become violent and the police having had to control them, including by shooting, nor had he witnessed injuries or arrests. He testified that he first learned of police brutality in that demonstration from reading the documents that the Minister disclosed. Asked how so, he explained that he hadn't read the news; he would work, practise martial arts and then go home.3 He added later that the newspapers could write what they wished, for him there had been neither injuries nor deaths at the demonstration.

The RPD found it inconsistent and not credible that Mr. XXXX had not been aware that "tens" of people had been killed and hundreds wounded by the security forces, including police, during the June 2001 demonstration. This was because he is an educated person and had continued in the XXXX XXXX for fourteen years after these events.4

The RPD's summary of the documentary evidence regarding the June 2001 demonstration is inaccurate. The evidence is that there were two to four killed, not tens.5 Over three hundred were injured. The documents the RPD cited referred to there having been 50 to 80 deaths earlier in 2001, and in Kabylia, not Algiers6.The Kabyles are a Berber people indigenous to Kabylia, about 150 kilometres east of Algiers.

According to Mr. XXXX uncontradicted evidence, he was stationed from 2001 to 2007 in Ghaia and Algers. He testified that the only 2001 demonstration at which he was present was the June 14 one in Algiers. A January 2002 report by Human Rights Watch explains what had happened in Kabylia that led up to it: More than ninety Algerians were reported killed during street protests that began on April 21 and continued sporadically for months. The demonstrations were sparked by the death on April 20 of Berber high school student Guermah Massinissa, who, two days earlier, had been shot while in custody in a gendarme barracks. Local youths rejected gendarmerie claims that the shooting was accidental and alleged that the gendarmes had increasingly harassed the local population in the preceding months. Many of the protests in the Kabylie were peaceful but in others, protesters threw stones or Molotov cocktails at gendarmes, and damaged public buildings and property, as well as private businesses. During the first and bloodiest week, gendarmes repeatedly opened fire on protesters without warning, using live ammunition. They also beat wounded persons and others not involved in the protests, according to many eyewitnesses. The demonstrators demanded, among other things, recognition of the Berber language and cultural identity and the withdrawal of the gendarmes from the region. In June, the street rallies spread to other regions, fueled by local grievances over corruption, joblessness, and housing allocations. On April 30, President Bouteflika announced an independent probe into the events. On May 2, he named a respected jurist, Mohand Issad, to head it. The commission's interim report, made public three months later, contrasted favourably with previous government-ordered inquiries that either were whitewashes or never came out at all. The commission found that the gendarmes had "kept the pot boiling by shooting live ammunition, ransacking, plundering, provocations of every sort, obscene language, and beatings." It concluded that self-defense claims could not justify the gendarmes' fatal shooting of fifty civilians and the wounding of another 218 by gunfire between April 22 and 28. During this period, it noted, one security force member died, by electrocution, although many were injured. The commission's interim report did not identify gendarmes or officers responsible for the excessive use of lethal force. Issad promised to resume the inquiry in August, but further findings were unavailable as this report went to press.

The gendarmerie are a paramilitary force under Algeria's Department of Defence. The XXXX, to whom Mr. XXXX belonged throughout his career, are a civil force under the Interior Department. As Counsel submits, citing the above numerous other reports in the RPD record, the civilian deaths in Kabylia were carried out by the gendarmes. This also applies to the torture or sexual abuse of Kabyle detainees,7 upon which the RPD placed much emphasis. I agree with the RPD that Mr. XXXX, who is Kabyle himself,8 would probably have heard about the civilian deaths in Kabylia by the time he was stationed at the June 14, 2001 demonstration in Algiers. Nevertheless, the fact that they were carried out by another force in another region puts considerable distance between him and those apparent crimes.

In 2001, Mr. XXXX was a member of a unit whose most important function, as he described it, was to act as XXXX XXXX. In that connection, Human Rights Watch noted: Shortly after President Bouteflika's address on April 30, security forces began showing greater restraint in their use of live ammunition. Authorities also reassigned many of the troops suspected of acting harshly, and deployed riot police units who used teargas more than live bullets. These factors helped to reduce casualties despite the larger and more widespread nature of the protests during May and June. On May 2l and 31, huge demonstrations were held, first in Tizi-Ouzou, then in Algiers. But on June 14, a Berber-dominated march of about half a million people in the capital degenerated into looting of shops and clashes involving the police, demonstrators, and local youth. Over three hundred were injured and four killed. Many of the hundreds detained by police were unaccounted for during several days; however, all were eventually released.

Again, I agree with the RPD that, as a XXXX XXXX XXXX present at the Algiers demonstration on June 14, Mr. XXXX must have come to know about the violence and casualties that happened there. His testimony to the contrary meant that he neither witnessed nor was briefed about it. That was not credible.

Given, however, that according to the reports before the RPD there were between half a million and a million demonstrators, of whom two to four were killed, and the large number of police units and officers who must have been present, it would not in my view be justified to conclude that there are serious reasons to believe that Mr. XXXX committed or made a significant contribution to a crime against humanity in connection with the June 14, 2001 demonstration or the June 2001 demonstrations in general. The Minister or the RPD must provide or base its decision on evidence that is individuated, rather than based on assumptions about collective guilt or innocence. In that context, I disagree with the inferences the RPD drew on this question. Exclusion - factors and evidentiary burden

When determining whether a person's conduct meets the requirements for complicity, the following list of non-exhaustive factors serves as a guide in assessing whether the person has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to a crime or criminal purpose: * the size and nature of the organization; * the part of the organization with which the refugee claimant was most directly concerned; * the refugee claimant's duties and activities within the organization; * the refugee claimant's position or rank in the organization; * the length of time the refugee claimant was in the organization, particularly after acquiring knowledge of the group's crime or criminal purpose; and * the method by which the refugee claimant was recruited and the refugee claimant's opportunity to leave the organization. * any viable defences (for example, duress).

Our Courts emphasize that the analysis of the factors is highly contextual and that the weighing of the factors has one key purpose in mind: to determine whether there was a voluntary, significant, and knowing contribution to a crime or criminal purpose. The factors are intended for guidance and not all of them will be relevant in every case.

It must be borne in mind that the evidentiary burden falls on the party seeking the refugee claimant's exclusion. For inquisitorial tribunals like the RPD and RAD, that burden may alternatively be carried by the tribunal itself. In either case, it does not fall on the claimant. Size and nature of the organization

The Algerian police (sûreté nationale) is a very large organization. It numbers about 200,000 members. That size can decrease the likelihood that an individual officer would have known of or participated in the crimes or criminal purpose of the organization. As the Algerian police force is multifaceted or heterogeneous, i.e., one that performs both legitimate and criminal acts, the link between the contribution and the criminal purpose will be more tenuous. The part of the organization with which the refugee claimant was most directly concerned

This factor may be relevant if particular parts of the organization were known to be involved with the crime or criminal purpose. For example, where only one part of the organization in question was involved in the crime or criminal purpose, a claimant's exclusive affiliation with another part(s) of the organization may serve to exonerate them for the purpose of art. 1F(a).

Mr. XXXX was affiliated with two parts of the XXXX XXXX: First, the XXXX XXXX XXXXt. After training, his active service with that unit was from 2001 to 2007. He then served with the XXXX XXXX XXXX in Algiers until 2015.9 He said that he worked for the latter's XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.10

There was almost no reference in the documentary evidence filed or the NDP to the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.11 Mr. XXXX testified that its most important function was to deal with demonstrations or riots.12 He said the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

Mr. XXXX description of the latter function was limited mainly to detecting stolen vehicles. It does not seem credible, however, that a rapid intervention unit would be deployed to set up road checkpoints merely for that purpose, which ordinary or even traffic police could handle. Given the unit's name and the documentary evidence about the roles of other Algerian special intervention or rapid response police squads,13 it is more likely that these roadblocks had a broader security purpose. The refugee claimant's duties and activities within the organization.

This factor is likely to be significant in any analysis of complicity, because it goes to the heart of a claimant's day-to-day participation in the activities of the organization. The RPD and RAD should consider the link between the duties and activities of a claimant, and the crimes and criminal purposes of the organization. Rapid intervention unit 2001-2007

In a form he filled out when making his refugee claim, Mr. XXXX wrote that his position in the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX", and that his functions were XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX14 As noted above, he testified that the unit's main purpose dealt with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX As for himself, he said that his role as "XXXX XXXX XXXX" was mostly routine XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He had no documents to corroborate that and said they don't exist.15 He testified that in fact the June 14, 2001 XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was the only one he had attended in the course of his duties. He did add that he participated in XXXX XXXX about ten to fifteen times when other XXXX were on leave.16 His actions there, as he described them, seemed to consist mainly of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX that were stolen until other specialized police arrived to take them to their stations.

As noted, Mr. XXXX testified that he had only ever worked at one demonstration.17 Although he had been issued a gun like any other XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, he said he was not authorized to bring it to demonstrations and had never used it except for target practice. Although a minority of police forces in the world do not carry arms unless the situation suggests in advance that they will be needed, one would probably consider that lack of weaponry unlikely at a major demonstration in Algeria where officers were tasked with preventing the crowd from reaching the presidential palace. Nevertheless, there was no inconsistency in this testimony, and I cannot find it implausible. Mr. XXXX was, he said, equipped with a shield and baton, but no handcuffs or tear gas, at the demonstration. He asserted that he had acted calmly towards the demonstrators, speaking to them in Kabyle and trying to reason with them. From the accounts of the event in the documents, things obviously went far beyond that, the demonstration developing into a riot. Again, however, given its vast size and the relatively low percentage of casualties, I cannot find it implausible.

The RPD correctly found Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was frequently notably vague. He often did not answer the precise question asked, even when it was rephrased several times. In addition, when asked what happened to persons he detained at roadblocks, and his role in that, he gave a long-drawn-out and convoluted series of answers18 that left the RPD member incredulous.19

Nevertheless, in exclusion proceedings the claimant is a defendant. That means, unlike inclusion, that the claimant's lack of credibility in his evidence, no matter how extensive, is not determinative. It simply means that that evidence does not advance his side of the argument against the allegations. In no way does it establish those allegations. That burden remains throughout strictly on the Minister or the RPD. Simply not believing the testimony does not fulfill that burden. That is, in fact, precisely why the Minister's representative conceded at the end of the testimony that the Minister could not establish that Mr. XXXX should be excluded under Article 1F(a).20

The report in the archived NDPs on human rights in Algeria closest to Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is the UK's Foreign and Commonwealth Office August 2010 Human Rights Assessment of Algeria. It stated: Between 1992 and 2000 disappearances were a common occurrence. Both the army and security forces have been accused of involvement in disappearances. We are confident that disappearances no longer take place as the rule of law returned to Algeria at the end of the civil war [early 2002]. The media has not reported any recent cases of enforced or involuntary disappearance.21

The same report also observed: The police and justice system is relatively incorrupt in the main urban centres, although corruption is a growing problem, especially in rural areas where petty corruption is more commonplace than in the big cities... The police generally respect human rights, although many international bodies continue to criticise past abuses. US State Department has reported accusations against the police of torture, impunity and arbitrary arrests/prolonged detention. We have seen no evidence to suggest that these claims are accurate in modern Algeria.22

This is a highly credible source. Although there are, as it notes, views to the contrary, the Foreign Office tends to establish that there are not serious reasons to believe that every Algerian police officer whose active service included the years 2001 to 2007 and who was stationed in the capital committed or was complicit, within the terms stipulated by the Supreme Court of Canada, in crimes against humanity. XXXX XXXX 2007-2015

As noted, Mr. XXXX testified that he worked in the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for over seven years. During that time, he said, he XXXX only about twenty people.23 Some had come to his office in response to being summoned, others he handcuffed and arrested in the field. He did interrogate them. He did this, he said, at his office; there was no special interrogation room. He never interrogated anyone in a prison. He denied using interrogation "techniques".24 He said he did not torture anyone, nor had he heard of any of his colleagues doing so.

Clearly having documentary evidence about widespread torture in most police stations in Algeria in mind, the Minister's representative and RPD member asked Mr. XXXX many questions about what happened to suspects whom he concluded after interrogation should be prosecuted. He answered that he did not transport the suspects to any police station. That was done by specialised police from other units whom he would call in for that purpose after XXXX XXXX XXXX. He stated that his XXXX XXXX XXXX had its own independent building and was not linked to any police station.
After the documentary evidence about torture in police stations was put to him, Mr. XXXX responded that he knew nothing of that and had no business to go there.25

The RPD found, correctly, that Mr. XXXX had not been clear in describing his powers of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Nevertheless, what the RPD found mattered was that he had the power to XXXX XXXX from 2007 to 2015 and had done so at least twenty times.26

The basis for the contention that torture is carried out in most Algerian police stations was a 2003 report by Algeria Watch.27 That report, however, is about the anti-Islamist "war" begun by the security forces in the early 1990s.28 While one might speculate that some suspects XXXX XXXX Mr. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX were implicated in that war, there is no evidence of that. In my opinion, the evidence did not establish serious reasons to believe that Mr. XXXX was aware that suspects he or his unit XXXX ended up being tortured at police stations. The refugee claimant's position or rank in the organization

A high-ranking individual in an organization may be more likely to have knowledge of that organization's crime or criminal purpose. In some cases, a high rank or rapid ascent through the ranks of an organization could evidence strong support of the organization's criminal purpose. Moreover, by virtue of their position or rank, individuals may have effective control over those directly responsible for criminal acts, possibly engaging criminal liability.

During his XXXX XXXX XXXX years to 2007, Mr. XXXX held the rank of "XXXX", XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX He entered XXXX XXXX XXXX with the same rank in 2007. He was promoted by one rank in December 2011 to XXXX.29 He testified that he XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

Mr. XXXX thus held lower ranks throughout his XXXX XXXX. The RPD emphasized, however, that he had served for 16 years (including training) and had progressively gained greater responsibilities, including leading "big investigations" into well-known and connected families within Algerian circles of power while with the XXXX XXXX.30

The RPD found that despite his low rank, Mr. XXXX contribution within the XXXX was recognized and significant. It followed, the Member held, that it was unlikely that Mr. XXXX had been unaware of the regular use of torture and the commission of other crimes against humanity by the XXXX XXXX.31

Counsel acknowledges there was evidence of torture and other serious crimes by members of the Algerian civil police. (This was the report on the events in Kabyle in the months before the June 2014 demonstration, and the 2003 Algeria Watch report, both of which I have analysed above.) She submits, however, that to meet the standard for exclusion, there must be evidence that the appellant had personal and knowing participation in the crime or criminal purpose of his organization. As per Ezokola, she adds, personal and knowing participation is more difficult to establish within a large and multifaceted organization, particularly when the claimant is a low-ranking member of a division not known to be directly involved with the organization's crime or criminal purpose.

The XXXX XXXX are not a limited brutal purpose organisation. I agree with counsel that Mr. XXXX low rank in a huge organisation that conducted many legitimate functions is not significantly offset by the fact that he did a good job carrying out one of them. The length of time the refugee claimant was in the organization, particularly after acquiring knowledge of the group's crime or criminal purpose

While the evidence may not establish Mr. XXXX personal participation in crimes against humanity, I agree with the RPD that fourteen years of active service in two divisions gave Mr. XXXX so much opportunity to hear of wrongdoing within XXXX XXXX that there is serious reason to believe he became aware of it. (Counsel did not make a submission on this point.)

Nevertheless, the focus in the cited documentary evidence on pre-2003 police crimes, together with the credible Foreign Office 2010 report that these had largely diminished after 2002, markedly lessens the negative impact of this factor. The method by which the refugee claimant was recruited and the refugee claimant's opportunity to leave the organisation

These two factors directly impact the voluntariness requirement. Mr. XXXX acknowledged that he joined the XXXX voluntarily, albeit faced with little opportunity to earn a living otherwise, in 1999. He also confirmed that he had been able to resign at any time, with no penalty other than loss of pension rights. He also said he would have accepted further promotions during his career had they been offered. His departure also was motivated by his alleged persecution by the XXXX XXXX after he denounced it for mismanagement and corruption, rather than any objection to crimes against humanity by the force.
The RPD was correct to find that there was no involuntariness or coercion in Mr. XXXX joining or remaining with the XXXX.
There is also no evidence of duress connected to Mr. XXXX activities in the XXXX XXXX. Conclusion - RPD erred

Having considered and balanced all the above factors and findings, I agree with the Minister that the evidence before the RPD and me was insufficient to establish that Mr. XXXX is excluded from refugee protection. The collective nature of some international crimes does not erase the importance of holding an individual responsible only for their own culpable acts. There was not evidence of direct or accomplice liability of Mr. XXXX for any crime against humanity; nor were there, in my opinion, serious reasons for considering him voluntarily to have contributed in a significant way to such crimes the Algerian state apparently committed. In particular, neither his rank, duties nor demonstrated acts, especially in divisions of a XXXX XXXX that is part of a very large and diverse set of security forces, meet that threshold, which is higher than mere reasonable grounds for suspecting.

The appeal is allowed. I send this matter back to the RPD to be redetermined by a different member.
